title: Indoor Acoustic Requirements for Autism-Friendly Spaces
research_question: To understand how to combine the acoustic necessities imposed by smart sensors and the acoustic indoor requirements presented by autistic people with hearing impairments or hypersensitivity to sound.
study_design: Mixed-methods study combining a literature review, on-site acoustic measurements in a real facility, and 3D acoustic simulations to optimize indoor sound fields.
participant_demographics: Not applicable for the experimental part (acoustic measurements/simulations). The literature review refers to autistic individuals, including children, teenagers, and adults.
environmental_context: A daily care facility dedicated to autistic individuals, featuring therapy rooms, a soft room, an atelier (art workshop), and residential bedrooms.
independent_variables: Room type (therapy room, soft room, atelier, bedroom)
Room configuration (empty, furnished, sound absorbing areas on ceiling, sound absorbing areas partially on corners and ceiling)
dependent_variables: Spatial distribution of RT, C50, D50
Just Noticeable Difference (JND) in acoustic parameters
measures: On-site impulse response measurements (ISO 3382-1 standard) for T30
3D acoustic ray tracing simulations for RT, C50, D50
Literature review of optimal acoustic parameters for sensors and autistic individuals

findings.antecedent: Indoor acoustic environment for autistic individuals (hearing impairment/hypersensitivity) and acoustic sensors
findings.consequent: Optimal acoustic parameters (Reverberation Time, Clarity Index, Definition)
findings.quote: the range RT = 0.4 ÷ 0.7 s... appears to be optimal for both the application of microphones and for subjects particularly sensitive to auditory stimuli. From the point of view of C50, the literature also suggests aiming at C50 ≥ 2 dB... while for D50, the selected range is... D50 ≥ 0.7.

findings.antecedent: Room size (small vs. large) and presence of furniture
findings.quote: small rooms... presented RT frequency values between 0.5 and 0.8 s; the largest rooms... depicted a volcano-shape pattern with higher values (RT > 1 s) at 500 Hz.

findings.antecedent: Indoor sound field distribution (spatial variation of RT, C50, D50)
findings.quote: the corner positions do not represent the optimal device locations... placing sensors adjacent to the ceiling is not the best choice because of the reverberation increasing. Preferably, an installation of several devices is suggested.

findings.antecedent: Soft room with sound-absorbing materials (polyurethane foams)
findings.consequent: Reverberation time and definition spatial distribution
findings.quote: Spatial distribution of reverberation time and definition at 1000 Hz frequency band... were quite good and it can be highlighted that when corner focusing is still present, the phenomenon is very limited... no JND was found.

findings.antecedent: Sound absorbing areas positioned only on the ceiling (configuration iii) in a small room (therapy room no. 4)
findings.quote: the reverberation time of the room decreases at 1000 Hz from 0.87 s (Figure 5) to 0.62 s (Figure 9, right) as a mean value

findings.antecedent: Sound absorbing areas positioned only on the ceiling (configuration iii) in a small room (therapy room no. 4)
findings.quote: the values of these parameters increased when moving from configuration (ii) (Table 1) to (iii)

findings.antecedent: Sound absorbing areas distributed partially on corners and ceiling (configuration iv) in a small room (therapy room no. 4)
findings.consequent: Spatial distribution of sound field and sensor range
findings.quote: A more distributed application of sound absorbing material eliminates focusing effects in corners and improves the sensor range and individuals' perception.

findings.antecedent: Empty bedroom vs. bedroom with furniture
findings.quote: a mean reverberation time value for the empty room at about 1.3 s at the 1000 Hz frequency... the inclusion of furnishing accessories in the room... led to a lower reverberation time (RT = 0.7 s at 1000 Hz).

findings.antecedent: Sound absorbing surface distributed only on the ceiling (iii) vs. partially on corners and ceiling (iv) in a bedroom
findings.consequent: Reverberation time (RT) at low frequencies, Clarity (C50), Definition (D50), spatial distribution, JND
findings.quote: The quality of indoor sound field distribution at the low and high frequency range improves if the sound absorbing material is located only on the ceiling. The sound focus in corners decreases significantly... configurations (iii) and (iv) suit the requirements of both autistic individuals and sensors, avoiding corners.

findings.antecedent: Empty atelier vs. atelier with furniture
findings.quote: The reverberation time for configuration (i) was about 2.9 s at 1000 Hz and decreased at about 0.9 s when inserting pieces of furniture as configuration (ii).

findings.antecedent: Sound absorbing surface distributed only on the ceiling (iii) vs. partially on corners and ceiling (iv) in an atelier (large room)
findings.consequent: Reverberation time (RT), Definition (D50), spatial distribution, JND
findings.quote: the reverberation decreased to 0.62 s in configuration (iii) and to 0.52 s in the (iv) one. In addition, sound focusing in corners decreased in the latter case... From the point of view of subjective perception, 10 JND occurs in (i) configuration, four in (ii), two in (iii), and only one in (iv).

discussion: The study highlights the importance of optimizing indoor acoustic environments for autistic individuals and acoustic sensors. It confirms that RT, C50, and D50 are key objective parameters. The optimal ranges for these parameters (RT: 0.4-0.7 s, C50 ≥ 2 dB, D50 ≥ 0.7) are derived from literature for both sensor performance and the needs of hearing-impaired individuals. The research demonstrates that existing rooms often fall outside these optimal ranges. Through simulations, it shows that while adding sound-absorbing materials generally improves acoustic parameters, the *distribution* of these materials is crucial for achieving homogeneous sound fields and minimizing JNDs, especially in large rooms. For small rooms, a continuous absorbing ceiling is preferred, while for large rooms, distributed absorption on corners and ceiling is more effective. The study also notes that visual discontinuities from acoustic panels might be a concern for autistic individuals, suggesting the need for masking surfaces. The findings emphasize a user-centered design approach, considering both the technical requirements of sensors and the sensory sensitivities of autistic occupants.
limitations: The study's JND analysis is mentioned, but specific methods or statistical significance of JNDs are not detailed.
The study focuses on specific room types and a single facility, which may limit the generalizability of the findings.
The research highlights the need to evaluate in detail the 'likes and dislikes' of autistic individuals, implying a lack of direct user feedback in this study's experimental design.
The visual impact of acoustic interventions (e.g., material discontinuities) is identified as a potential issue for autistic individuals, but not directly investigated in terms of user perception.
future_work: Further research is needed to evaluate in detail the likes and dislikes of autistic individuals regarding indoor acoustic environments and visual aspects of acoustic interventions.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Indoor Acoustic Requirements for Autism-Friendly Spaces
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: The architecture of spaces for people on the autistic spectrum is evolving toward inclusive design, which should fit the requirements for independent, autonomous living, and proper support for relatives and caregivers. The use of smart sensor systems represents a valuable support to internal design in order to achieve independent living for impaired people. Accordingly, these devices can monitor or prevent hazardous situations, ensuring security and privacy. Acoustic sensor systems, for instance, could be used in order to realize a passive monitoring system. The correct functioning of such devices needs optimal indoor acoustic criteria. Nevertheless, these criteria should also comply with dedicated acoustic requests that autistic individuals with hearing impairment or hypersensitivity to sound could need. Thus, this research represents the first attempt to balance, integrate, and develop these issues, presenting (i) a wide literature overview related to both topics, (ii) a focused analysis on real facility, and (iii) a final optimization, which takes into account, merges, and elucidates all the presented unsolved issues.
